newsitem.title: UK: Hong Kong's Lee defies colony's future leader.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Lee defies colony's future leader.

text.p: Hong Kong Democratic Party leader Martin Lee refused on Wednesday to back down in the face of criticism from the colony's Chinese-appointed future leader and vowed to speak out for human rights.

Lee said his party, the largest in the Legislative Council that China will dissolve when it resumes sovereignty of Hong Kong in 19 weeks time, had been elected because it had a good track record of speaking up for the colony.
He lashed out at Britain, the colonial ruler for 150 years, for "doing nothing" to safeguard Hong Kong's freedoms as the handover loomed.
Lee rejected attacks by future leader Tung Chee-hwa, who has accused him of blackening Hong Kong's name by spreading doomsday forecasts.

"If Hong Kong is in good shape, no bad-mouthing by anybody can hurt it," Lee said at a lunch at London's Foreign Press Association. "If it is in bad shape, then no amount of good-mouthing can save it."
He added: "When they are taking away our people's freedom, they want us to shut up, but I will not shut up."

Lee said he did not know if his outspoken criticisms of China would be considered subversive when Beijing takes over Hong Kong. Nor could he say if he would be allowed to speak out in Hong Kong after the handover.

Lee accuses China of breaking the 1984 agreement covering the return of Hong Kong by imposing an unelected provisional legislature. He has threatened to sue the body if it meets in Hong Kong, saying it is unconstitutional to have two legislatures operating at the same time.

Lee, on a tour of Europe to drum up support against China's planned rollback of freedoms in Hong Kong, warned business leaders that it was not in their interests to turn a blind eye to the erosion of human rights in the colony.
It was wrong to believe that Hong Kong could "be deprived of its freedoms and continue to lay golden eggs".
Even if companies only invested in China, it was wrong to assume that they would not be affected if human rights in Hong Kong, including press freedom, were lost after the handover.
Investment decisions about China could only be made on the basis of timely and accurate information and that was now only available in Hong Kong.
China, by contrast exaggerated good news about its economy and suppressed bad news, Lee said.
Lee said Britain had threatened to the International Court of Justice in The Hague but had in fact taken no action to safeguard human rights in Hong Kong.
Britain's policy was to blame China if anything went wrong with the Hong Kong handover at the end of June, while China could be expected to blame Britain.

"If Britain does not leave behind any institutions to enable the people of Hong Kong to maintain the rule of law, then the sun will set with shame on June 30 over the way we have been sewn up by the British," Lee said.
